analysis.investment_thesis: Kaynes is a genuinely impressive growth story in Indian EMS — revenue from INR 364 Cr to INR 2,722 Cr in six years is remarkable — but at 72x P/E with 10.7% ROE and INR -1,031 Cr free cash flow in FY25, I am being asked to pay an extraordinary price for a capital-hungry business that does not yet earn its cost of capital. Growth without returns is just burning money faster.
key_strengths: Exceptional revenue growth: 39.8% CAGR over 6 years, serving high-value end-markets (aerospace, defence, medical, railways)
Strong promoter conviction: 53.46% stake with management deeply invested in long-term outcomes
Low debt/equity of 0.19 relative to the scale of expansion underway; balance sheet not yet stressed
key_risks: ROE of only 10.7% — well below my 15% threshold — as heavy capex dilutes returns on the mushrooming equity base (INR 4,680 Cr FY25 vs INR 203 Cr FY22)
Free cash flow deeply negative: -INR 1,031 Cr in FY25, -INR 312 Cr in FY24, -INR 100 Cr in FY23 — the business consumes more cash than it generates
Capital intensity accelerating: capex jumped from INR 42 Cr (FY22) to INR 949 Cr (FY25), CWIP at INR 402 Cr — execution risk is high
red_flags: Paying 72x P/E for a business with sub-15% ROE violates the fundamental principle that price is what you pay, value is what you get
Finance costs tripling from INR 36 Cr to INR 106 Cr in two years as debt climbs to INR 903 Cr — the capital cycle may not deliver the promised returns
OCF only positive 3 of 5 years; a growth narrative dependent on perpetual equity raises and debt is not a business — it's a project
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The EMS sector in India has genuine secular tailwinds — defence indigenisation, PLI schemes, import substitution — and Kaynes is positioned to benefit. The 50% EBITDA CAGR and client diversification across mission-critical industries speak to real execution capability. I respect the promoters for building something from nothing since 1988.

However, at 72x earnings with a 10.7% ROE, the market has priced in perfection and then some. EMS is inherently a low-moat, capital-intensive, execution-dependent business — margins of 12.3% are thin and easily eroded by customer concentration, input cost shocks, or project delays. When I buy a business, I want it to be generating cash, not consuming it at INR 1,031 Cr per year. At half this price, the calculus might change; today, I'll pass.
